newsitem.title: INDIA: India's love of gold endures despite weak prices.
newsitem.headline: India's love of gold endures despite weak prices.

text.p: Indians' love of gold will endure despite the metal's lost lustre, reflected in prices at 12-year lows, economists and dealers said on Tuesday.
"I don't think my mother-in-law would stop holding on to gold because the prices have gone down," Ira Patnaik, a New Delhi-based economist, told Reuters.
"Its value for her is not going to decrease because of recent price fluctuations," Patnaik said, explaining gold's special place in India's social and cultural traditions.
India's main demand is for gold jewellery, given and used at an estimated 10 million weddings each year. This absorbs nearly 300 tonnes of the metal annually, bullion dealers said.
India's wedding season begins in November and lasts up to February.

Analysts say India's desire for gold has turned it into the world's largest consumer of the metal, although nearly a third of its 900 million people live below the poverty line with the average per capita income at around $330 a year.
India's annual consumption of gold is estimated at around 500 tonnes, most of it imported.
Official figures put the cost of gold imports in 1995 at $3.4 billion -- second only to oil in value.
The sharp fall in gold prices has fuelled investor fears that modern economies view their gold reserves as just another asset rather than a final repository of wealth, the role it used to enjoy.
But Indians' love for gold was likely to last, economists said.
"Gold will continue to be a valuable asset and I don't think there will be any significant realignments," said Shashank Bhide of the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).
He said the relative value of gold as an asset might decline only when the stock markets expanded to large levels, and that could take a long time.
In London, on Monday gold sank as low as $314.10 per ounce, down $10 from Friday's close, before recovering slightly to $318.
The gold price fell below $325 an ounce on Friday to its lowest in 12 years after news that Australia's central bank sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves.
Moving in the shadow of depressed world markets, gold prices fell sharply this week in the Indian subcontinent.
"This (price fall) is a good sign for India because it is a big buyer," said Makhan Lal Damani, president of the Bombay Bullion Association.
Damani said in calendar 1996, India imported more than 400 tonnes of gold and imports were expected to go beyond 500 tonnes this year.
Dealers said the daily buying in India had fallen to about 1,000 kg in the past fortnight from the normal 1,250 kg but they expected demand to reignite once prices began recovering.
"I don't think the craze for gold is going to go down," said economist Atul Sarma. "It is a kind of liquid asset."
Bhide said banks might not find it attractive to hold gold reserves but for individuals, it continued to be a solid asset and remained a hedge against inflation.
India's gold holdings are put at around 9,000 tonnes, accumulated from centuries of trading, and account for about seven percent of an estimated world stock of 128,000 tonnes.
